messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel, a 35-year-old Latin American musician, came to therapy after months of trying to keep his life looking normal since a road accident that had nearly killed him. He had been on his way home from a late-night gig when a truck ran a red light and slammed into his car, leaving him trapped, pinned, and waiting for help while sirens echoed somewhere beyond the twisted metal. He remembered the crush of the seatbelt, the smell of gasoline, and then only disconnected flashes: a shard of broken windshield glittering in the dark, a paramedic’s glove, his own voice shouting once and then fading. When he tried to remember the full sequence on purpose, it would not come; he was left with pieces that would not join up, and the missing parts felt more alarming than the fragments themselves. Daniel spoke of the crash as something deeply unfair, something that should have been prevented and for which nothing had ever truly been done. He had come to believe that the accident had destroyed the life he had built, and that anger sat close to the surface in him; he feared that if he let himself fully think about what happened, he would lose control of that rage and do something terrible.

In the weeks after the collision, Daniel began arranging his days around other people. He made sure there were always bandmates, friends, cousins, or neighbors around him, filling the apartment with noise and company so he would not be left alone with his thoughts. He accepted every invitation, lingered after rehearsals, stayed in diners long after meals were finished, and kept his phone busy with calls and messages. He did not want to talk about the accident or what came after it, and when anyone asked, he changed the subject, joked, or left the room. He told himself that conversation would only open the door to the anger he was trying to contain. The more he sensed the anger under the surface, the more insistently he stayed surrounded by people, as if constant socialising could keep him from the parts of himself he no longer trusted.

At the same time, the way the memory came to him made it harder to live with. Because he could not deliberately pull the crash into a clear sequence, Daniel filled in the gaps with his own fear, and what remained incomplete took on a punishing meaning. The unfinished fragments made him more certain that the event had ruined everything: if even his mind could not hold the whole story together, then the accident must have been as catastrophic as he felt. The missing pieces also fed his suspicion that something inside him had gone permanently wrong. He began to watch himself for signs of anger, convinced that he might suddenly lose control, and that belief made him even more determined not to sit still with the memory. He avoided thinking about the night of the crash, but that effort had its own cost. The more he tried not to go there, the less coherent the memory became, and the more it seemed to confirm that the event was beyond repair and beyond justice.

Daniel’s musical work and home life became the settings for this pattern. In rehearsal spaces, backstage rooms, and at home after his wife had gone to bed, he worked hard to keep moving, keep talking, keep the room occupied. If the conversation slowed, he reached for another story, another drink, another reason to stay with someone. Yet each burst of company left him less able to settle the fragments of the accident into words or sequence, and the memory stayed just out of reach. That, in turn, made the injustice and the sense of ruin feel even larger. He said he could not understand how his life, once built around music, family, and late-night energy, could have been broken so violently, and he was frightened by how readily his mind returned to the thought that everything had been taken from him.

By the time he sought help, Daniel was exhausted by the cycle. He no longer trusted quiet moments, and he was afraid that if he kept avoiding the memory he would remain trapped in the same incomplete, angry state, but if he opened it up he might be overwhelmed by rage he could not control. What brought him in was the realization that his constant company-seeking, his refusal to speak about the crash, and his efforts to avoid thinking about it were no longer just helping him get through the day; they were keeping the accident alive in pieces that felt more threatening than the truth. He hoped therapy might help him make sense of what happened, and he was most afraid that the life he believed had been destroyed would stay that way forever.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows negative beliefs about the accident, but it does not clearly state that these appraisals drive the fragmented/incomplete memory.
The vignette describes fragmented memory leading to worse beliefs about the crash, but it does not clearly show the memory causing the negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
The vignette shows avoidance and constant company-seeking, but it does not clearly state that these maladaptive strategies cause the memory to become less coherent or more fragmented.
